Introduction to the course In many professional fields we are frequently confronted with the need to best utilize a limited amount of available resources. When, as in most cases, it is possible to define a standard of assessment permitting to compare and to arrange in an order the existing alternatives, we are essentially facing an optimization problem. The solution of this kind of problems requires first of all an abstraction phase (conceptualization or modeling of the system to be optimized) and secondly the application of appropriate mathematical tools and algorithms in order to determine a solution supporting the final choice. The purpose of this course is to provide the fundamental operational elements of the different modeling and optimization techniques and, at the same time, to present a certain number of tools useful to describe and to solve a wide range of optimization problems, with special attention to problems arising in information technology, telecommunications and transportation. The techniques and the methodological tools on which this course is based are those of Operations Research. Beside model-building aspects, which will be examined making use of a specific modeling language and of professional software, we will also study the algorithmic aspects by introducing the main methods for solving optimization problems representable through graphs and network flows. Moreover, we will examine the fundaments of Linear Programming and of Integer Linear Programming, which will be the object of deeper analysis in later courses. The paragraphs and examples marked with an asterisk * are meant as closer investigations and are here discussed in relation to the specific field of interest of this course. Bibliographic references For a deeper study of model-building aspects and the use of Mosel language, we suggest: Guéret, C., Prins, C. and Servaux, M. Applications of Optimization with Xpress-MP. Dash Optimization ltd. (www.dashoptimization.com), 2002. Williams, H. P. Model Building in Mathematical Programming. Wiley, 3rd edition, 1995. For a deeper study of models and algorithms on graphs and network flows, see: Ahuja, R. K., Magnanti, T. L. and Orlin, J. B. Network Flows. Theory, Algorithms, and Applications. Prentice Hall, 1993. Concerning Linear Programming we suggest the consultation of: Bertsimas, D. and Tsitsiklis, J. Introduction to Linear Optimization. Athena Scientific, 1996. Concerning aspects of computational complexity and the analysis of algorithms, we suggest: Papadimitrou, C. H. and Steiglitz, K. Combinatorial Optimization. Algorithms and Complexity. Prentice Hall, 1982. For a deeper study of Integer Linear Programming, see: Wolsey, L. A. Integer Programming. Wiley, 1998.

Federico Malucelli Introduction to Operations Research - 2 - Optimization Models

# Page 3^page=3
Federico Malucelli Introduction to Operations Research - 3 - 1 What does it mean to optimize? If we attentively consider everyday life, we notice that the idea of optimizing is much more widespread than we expect and that it is inherent in human behavior and even in the natural system. How many times does it happen that we try to achieve the best result with the minimum effort or to accomplish a task within the shortest possible time or to best utilize the resources we have at our disposal in working, studying, doing sports or playing a game? Let us start from the latter case in order to understand the difficulties arising when we approach optimization problems with a method. Example: a construction game We have an assemblage kit containing pieces of different colors and dimensions, each corresponding to a specific component of a mobile phone. We have: 10 display modules (blue- colored); 18 memory modules (green-colored); 12 transmission modules (yellow-colored); 21 six- key keypads (red-colored); 9 navigation keyboards (white-colored); 10 microcameras (pink- colored). Appropriately combining these elements, we can assemble mobile phones of two different models, as shown below: Model A Model B Fig. 1: the two models of mobile phones to be assembled Each phone of type A brings 3 points; each phone of type B brings 8 points. The game consists in assembling the pieces that we have, trying to make the highest possible score. Keeping the various components at our disposal, it is not difficult to generate feasible solutions, that is combinations of pieces satisfying the “recipes” of mobile phones, and it can be easy to quickly detect among all possible combinations the one making the highest score. But it is certainly not so easy to certify that the chosen solution is the very best – something we can efficiently do only by using mathematical tools – or to quantify the intrinsic value of resources (for example: how much are we ready to pay for one more keyboard?), or to assess the solution stability in case of

# Page 4^page=4
Federico Malucelli Introduction to Operations Research - 4 - variations of the granted points. All this, of course in addition to the determination of the best solution, is the aim pursued by using Operations Research methods. 2 Operations Research The object of Operations Research is the study, the creation and the adjustment of methods and of quantitative tools for solving decision-making problems. First used in the military sector during the Second World War, Operations Research found immediate application in a variety of fields, such as logistics, production, transportation, telecommunications, finance. At the present day, which is characterized by extremely dynamic and complex contexts, Operations Research has become a must-have tool for supporting the decision-making process. The typical problems that are approached by means of Operations Research are those implying decisions when small amounts of resources are available, that is when a given set of constraints is to be respected while maximizing the “benefit” coming from the use of those resources. These problems are also defined optimization problems. The following table exemplifies a few optimization problems that emerged in various application fields and were solved thanks to Operations Research tools. These examples are drawn from the list of the finalist works of the Franz Edelman Award, which is granted once a year by the international community to the most outstanding Operations Research applications. More information is available on the site of INFORMS, the American association of Operations Research (www.science ofbetter.org). year company sector effect 86 Eletrobras Hydroelectric power 43M$ annual saving 90 Taco Bell Personnel shifts 7.6M$ annual saving 92 Harris (semiconductors) Production planning on a global scale 50%⇒95% “on time” orders 95 GM - Car Rental Utilization of the fleet of cars +50M$ a year, business failure avoided 96 HP - Printers Replanning of a production line production doubled 99 IBM Reorganization of a logistic chain 750M$ annual saving 00 Syngenta Corn seeds production 5M$ annual saving Table 1: examples of OR applications 3 How to approach an optimization problem If we observe our everyday life, we realize how frequently we are confronted with optimization problems, for example when we determine the best route to go to work, or we go shopping minimizing the time we spend and not exceeding the available budget, or again when we organize our activities without waste of time, etc. If the solution of such everyday problems does not necessarily imply the recourse to the quantitative tools provided by Operations Research (and

# Page 5^page=5
Federico Malucelli Introduction to Operations Research - 5 - perhaps this would be boring), these tools cannot be ignored when solving problems with a higher degree of complexity and a far-reaching impact; for example: to determine the route of a regular city bus so as to maximize the quality of the service or the number of transported passengers, to plan the personnel shifts so as to minimize costs, to manage the securities portfolio of an investment fund so as to minimize the risk while maximizing the expected return. Intuition and common sense are frequently not enough to solve this kind of problems and, anyhow, common sense and intuition are not able to guarantee the effective quality of the chosen solution. The following example shows a production-planning problem whose formulation is rather simple, but whose solution is far from evident. Example: a cosmetics firm Employing the same raw material as a basis, a cosmetics firm produces a cream for the body (Body) and a cream for the face (Face), both in two versions: standard (Regular) and luxurious (Luxury). The cost of the raw material is 3 € per kilogram; to turn a kilogram of raw material into the Regular product requires an hour of work. A kilo of raw material gives 4 hectograms of Body Regular and 3 hectograms of Face Regular, that are sold at 6 and 7 € per hectogram, respectively. Moreover, it is possible to improve the fragrance, the color and the package of the two creams by producing the Luxury versions from the Regular versions. To turn one hectogram of Regular Body into one hectogram of Luxury Body takes 4 additional hours of work and 4 € ; the selling price of Luxury Body is 14 € per hectogram. Likewise, to turn one hectogram of Regular Face into one hectogram of Luxury Face takes 3 additional hours of work and 4 € ; the selling price of Luxury Face is 18 € per hectogram. Knowing that he has at his disposal no more than 6,000 hours of manpower and that he can buy no more than 4,000 kilograms of basis raw material, the product manager wishes to plan the production so as to maximize the profits. A decision-making process can be schematically divided into the following phases: 1) detection of the decision-making problem; 2) fact analysis and data collection; 3) model building as an abstraction of the real problem; 4) determination of one or more solutions; 5) analysis of the results obtained and their interpretation in relation to the real case. The phases mentioned above are not necessarily in sequence; actually, feedback is often to be taken into account, because the results of a certain phase may suggest changes in the choices made in the previous phases. Along this course we will focus on model building, on the development of efficient algorithms for solving models or on the use of commercial optimization software and on the interpretation of the resulting solutions.

# Page 6^page=6
Federico Malucelli Introduction to Operations Research - 6 - The model is an abstraction permitting to describe in “mathematical” terms the outstanding features of the problem we want to study and solve. The formulation of a model implies three fundamental points: 1) detection of the decisions pertaining to the examined problem. In the cosmetics firm example, the decisions to be made concern: the quantity of raw material to be bought, the quantity of the different creams to be produced, the number of working hours. In a mathematical kind of model decisions are represented by decision variables; 2) determination of the objective or objectives to be optimized. In the cosmetics firm example the objective is to maximize the profit, that is the difference between the earnings brought by the creams’ sales and the costs (the working cost and the purchase of raw material) involved to produce them. It is generally possible to express the objective as a function of the decision variables (objective function); 3) definition of feasible solutions. In practice, we wish to express the “rules” defining the decision- making problem. In the case of the cosmetics firm, for example, we know that the working hours cannot be more than 6,000 or that in order to produce one hectogram of face cream we need 1/3 kilogram of raw material. These relations are generally called constraints of the problem. Models can be divided into three main classes: mathematical programming models; game theory models; simulation models. In mathematical programming models the entire system to be examined is described using mathematical (or logical) relations between variables representing the elements of the system; therefore, solving the problem implies seeking those values of the decision variables that satisfy the constraints and maximize or minimize the objective function. In game theory models the difficulty to mathematically represent the behavior of individuals or of the groups of individuals existing in the investigated reality is overcome by directly introducing man into the model through the “players”, each of whom is assigned a fixed role he has to play according to a certain strategy. A typical example is the study of economic markets or the study of cars traffic on an urban road network. Simulation models are generally employed when the investigated reality is very complex and also the data needed to study the problem are uncertain and affected by a large variability. In this case, we try to reproduce in the most accurate possible way the behavior of the system we want to examine by means of mathematical relations; then we proceed to study, on computer, its response to stimulations exerted with the help of generators of pseudo casual numbers, so as to make them as similar as possible to real stimulations. Simulation models are used to perform scenario analyses, which are also called “what if” analyses.

# Page 7^page=7
Federico Malucelli Introduction to Operations Research - 7 - When we interpret the results of models – no matter of which type – we must never forget that they are an abstraction of reality, therefore they might not reproduce all the details needed to approach the real problem: the solution obtained from the model is in fact the solution of the representation we have built of the real problem. It is strictly necessary to consider with the utmost attention the soundness of the model: the model will always correspond to a very limited description of reality, nonetheless it will have to represent with reasonable accuracy the aspects relevant to the solution of the decision-making problem we are confronted with. 4 Example of how to solve an optimization problem The following example shows first of all what are the steps leading to the solution of an optimization problem, then the building of the mathematical model starting from the problem description, and finally the detection of a solution method fully utilizing the properties of the model. We will build the model in a strict way, while the solution will be more empirical, but the method, guided by the directions of the mathematical model, will be nevertheless correct. Definition and analysis of the problem A farmer has at his disposal 12 hectares of land to plant with lettuce or potatoes. In addition to the land, he has at his disposal the following resources: 70 kg of lettuce seeds; 18 tonnes of tubers, 160 tonnes of manure to fertilize the soil. Supposing that the market is capable to use up the entire output and that the prices are stable, the estimated return of lettuce cultivation is 3,000 € per hectare and that of potato cultivation 5,000 € per hectare. The absorption of resources for each type of culture is: 7 kg of seeds and 10 tonnes of manure per hectare of lettuce; 3 tonnes of tubers and 20 tonnes of manure per hectare of potatoes. The problem facing the farmer is to decide how much land should be devoted to lettuce and how much to potatoes, so as to maximize the economic return and best utilize the available resources. Building of the mathematical model The decision variables are the quantity of hectares to be devoted to lettuce (xL) and the quantity of hectares to be devoted to potatoes (xP). Given a solution (xL, xP), the economic return is quantified by the objective function we intend to maximize: max 3000 xL + 5000 xP. The constraints are represented by the availability of resources and by their absorption due to cultivation. Hence, the number of cultivated hectares cannot exceed 12: xL + xP ≤ 12; the lettuce seeds and the tubers employed – which strictly depend on the number of hectares devoted to one or to the other culture – cannot exceed the availability, so: 7 xL ≤ 70 for the lettuce seeds, and for the tubers:

# Page 8^page=8
Federico Malucelli Introduction to Operations Research - 8 - 3 xP ≤ 18; the manure employed for both types of cultures cannot exceed the availability: 10 xL + 20 xP ≤ 160. Further, we should not forget the non-negativity constraints on the variables, because a negative quantity of land cannot be cultivated: xL , xP ≥ 0. Summing up, the complete model results as follows: max 3000 xL + 5000 xP xL + xP ≤ 12 7 xL ≤ 70 3 xP ≤ 18 10 xL + 20 xP ≤ 160 xL , xP ≥ 0. Problem solution Among all attributions of values to the variables xL and xP satisfying the constraints mentioned above, we have to detect the one totalizing the largest economic return. In order to do this, we proceed guided by the mathematical model. Considering all the constraints of the problem – and given that the system is made of 2-variable inequalities – we can draw its representation on the Cartesian plane by making the variable xL correspond to the abscissa axis and the variable xP to the ordinate axis. The edge of each constraint corresponds to a straight line. For example, the straight line xL + xP ≤ 12 corresponds to the edge of the constraint concerning the available hectares. The feasible half-plane is the one descending on the left side of the straight line. If we consider the other constraints as well, we can complete the representation of the feasible region. In Figure 2 the shaded region is defined by the intersection of all half-planes representing the constraints.

# Page 9^page=9
Federico Malucelli Introduction to Operations Research - 9 - xP xL (0,6) (10,0)(0,0) 10 xL+20x P =160 3xP =18 xL+ x P =12 (10,2) (8,4) (4,6) Fig. 2: geometric representation and solution of the farmer problem Any point belonging to the feasible region corresponds to a possible combination of the two cultures. These solutions are obviously innumerable; in order to find the best one we can restrict the range of research by remarking that the optimal solution must exploit at least one resource to the utmost extent. This means that in our research we can concentrate on the points belonging to the edge of the feasible region, or better still, pushing further the above remark, we can concentrate only on vertices. Among all vertices, given the nature of the solution evaluation function having positive coefficients, we can certainly reject the origin (corresponding to a solution yielding 0) and points ⎣ ⎡ ⎦ ⎤0 6 and ⎣ ⎡ ⎦ ⎤10 0 , dominated by ⎣ ⎡ ⎦ ⎤4 6 and ⎣ ⎡ ⎦ ⎤10 2 , respectively. Now we just have to evaluate the solutions corresponding to the points ⎣ ⎡ ⎦ ⎤4 6 , ⎣ ⎡ ⎦ ⎤8 4 and ⎣ ⎡ ⎦ ⎤10 2 : xL xP value 4 6 42000 8 4 44000 10 2 40000 Table 2: evaluation of solutions Consequently, the optimal solution is the one implying 8 hectares planted with lettuce and 4 with potatoes. Evidently, the method used to solve the farmer problem can hardly be used to solve problems with more than 2 or 3 variables. This is because even if it were possible to detect the vertices of the polyhedron corresponding to the feasible region, their number might be very high and therefore their evaluation would become quite expensive in terms of time. In fact, given a Rn polyhedron described by the intersection of m half-planes corresponding to the inequalities defining the

# Page 10^page=10
Federico Malucelli Introduction to Operations Research - 10 - problem constraints, the number of vertices could potentially get to ⎝ ⎛ ⎠ ⎞m n , because a vertex corresponds to the intersection of n linearly independent straight lines chosen among the m corresponding to the edges of the polyhedron. Later in the course we will consider some effective techniques to solve this class of problems. Such solution methods will also provide additional information concerning the solution, for instance the value of resources – i.e., the effect of the growth of some resources on the value of the optimal solution – or the solution stability in front of variations of the objective function coefficients. Exercise Give the geometric representation and the optimal solution of the problem of mobile phones. 5 Building mathematical optimization models The building of a mathematical model as an abstraction of a real problem is a complicated process which is difficult to systematize. Actually, it is based on experience, intuition and imagination: capabilities not easy to teach with traditional methods. Let us review some elements that can be used in defining mathematical models, with special attention to variables, constraints and objective functions. To do this, rather than giving general rules, we will make a general survey by examples. 5.1 Variables As shown in the above examples, variables represent decisions. In the cases more based on intuition – such as the farmer example and the game of mobile phones – variables represent absolute quantities: the number of hectares to be planted with lettuce or potatoes, the number of mobile phones of each model to be assembled. Variables of this type can be subjected to constraints concerning the sign or the nature of variables. In particular, both in the farmer case and in the mobile phone case the variables are restricted to take non-negative values because in the examined problems it is meaningless to cultivate a negative quantity of land or to produce a negative number of mobile phones. In other cases, it might have a meaning to consider variables restricted to assume non-positive values, or to consider free variables. The latter case can be exemplified as follows. Example: optimization of the train timetable Given a set of trains T={1,…,n} and a set of railway stations where the trains stop S={1,…,m}, we know the arrival times ats for each pair (t,s), t∈T, s∈S. The purpose is to study the effect of introducing variations in arrival times. So we introduce the variables πts representing perturbations in the given times. The new time of train t at station s is given by ats + πts. Since the variation could be whether a delay (πts>0) or an advance (πts<0) or null, the variables πts will be free. Another restriction concerning variables is the one relative to their nature. In the case of mobile phones it is quite obvious to restrict the attention to solutions capable to assemble an integer number of phones, since the possible fractions would have no value. Then we have the case of integer variables. The solution of integer variable problems is much more complicated than the solution of problems in which variables are continuous, as we shall see later on.

# Page 11^page=11
Federico Malucelli Introduction to Operations Research - 11 - Another frequent case is that of variables representing relative quantities. Let us analyze it with an example. Example: capital investment Consider the problem of deciding how to invest a capital of 137 k€ having at our disposal the financial instruments appearing in Table 3, each characterized by a maximum quantity to be purchased and by the size of the interest coupon: instrument 1 2 3 4 5 maximum availability in kE 40 12 130 5 400 coupon in k€ 3.2 1.5 4.2 0.7 17 Table 3: characteristics of the financial instruments The decisions to be made concern the quantity of each financial instrument one intends to purchase (xi, i=1,…,5). This time, instead of indicating an absolute value whose upper bound should change for each variable, variables xi represent the relative value of each purchased fund, so that they take values comprised between 0 and 1. The use of such variables can be easily understood looking at the complete model of the problem, which obviously aims at maximizing the earnings resulting from the interests drawn in proportion to the investment, while satisfying the constraint of not exceeding the available budget. max 3.2x1 + 1.5x2 + 4.2x3 + 0.7x4 + 17x5 40x1 + 12x2 + 130x3 + 5x4 + 400x5 ≤ 137 0 ≤ xi ≤ 1, i = 1, ..., 5. Variables representing relative values are often used in formulating network routing problems (on road or telecommunications networks); they describe the percentage of traffic circulating on each network link. Exercise Formulate the investment problem using variables representing absolute values and point out the differences from the above presented model. If we impose integrity constraints on variables representing relative values, we actually constrain the variables to take value 0 or 1, thus giving them a logical meaning. Therefore, in the case of the investment problem it would be necessary either altogether to choose or to reject the different instruments. The same problem can be more easily understood if we think of objects, as in the following example. Example: burglar A burglar secretly breaks into a jeweler’s shop carrying with him an empty bag having a capacity of 8 kilograms. He finds within his reach six objects whose value vi – calculated in thousands of Euros – is 7, 2, 4, 5, 4 and 1, respectively; whereas their weight pi is 5, 3, 2, 3, 1 and 1 kg, respectively. In

# Page 12^page=12
Federico Malucelli Introduction to Operations Research - 12 - order to carry the stolen goods in the only bag he has, he needs to make a choice of objects maximizing the global value. We can represent the problem in two ways. The first way is based on sets. Let O={1,2,3,4,5,6}, our decision variable is given by the set S⊆O; we wish to find a subset S such as to give ∑ i∈S pi ≤8 and such as to maximize ∑ i∈S vi . Alternatively, we can introduce a choice variable xi for each object i∈O having value 1 if and only if object i is chosen and having value 0 else. Decision variables are of a “logical” kind, i.e., for each object we have to decide whether to include it in the solution or not: xi has value 1 if the object i∈S and has value 0 else. The problem is then represented by the following model: max 7x1 + 2x2 + 4x3 + 5x4 + 4x5 + x6 5x1 + 3x2 + 2x3 + 3x4 + x5 + x6 ≤ 8 xi ∈ {0,1} , i = 1, ..., 6. Sometimes it may be necessary to make a choice among a finite set of values; the variable representing such a choice does not fall within any of the categories mentioned above, therefore we have to use a discrete value variable. Its typical contexts are telecommunications networks. Example: capacity of a telecommunications network In dimensioning telecommunications networks a frequent problem is the allocation of transmission capacities to the direct links between two centers. Considered a link l, the variable used to decide the capacity of such link is wl, which can only take one among the values d1 , d2 ,…, dr being typical of the transmission capacity and depending on the adopted technology: wl ∈{d1 , d2 ,…, dr }. This characteristic can be expressed by introducing r logical variables {0,1} corresponding to whether one of the r capacity values is chosen or not and by setting the real variable wl equal to the following expression: wl = d1 y1 + d2 y2 + … + dr yr . Obviously, it is necessary to add a constraint ensuring that only one of the values d1 , d2 ,…, dr is assigned to the variable wl, i.e., : y1 + y2 + … + yr = 1. In the latter case it already arises the need to introduce some constraints in order to enable variables to take the wanted meaning: something to be more deeply examined in the next paragraph. For the moment, let us briefly deal with the transformations to which variables can be subjected. A first, simple transformation concerns the sign of variables. If a variable x is restricted to take non- positive values and, for notational convenience or for other reasons, we need to have a non-negative variable in the model, we can introduce a new variable x', that we set equal to -x, and we can perform the due substitutions in the entire model. The new variable x' is restricted to take non-

# Page 13^page=13
Federico Malucelli Introduction to Operations Research - 13 - negative values. The same transformation may as well occur in the opposite direction, i.e., transforming a non-negative variable into a non-positive one. Greater attention requires the transformation of a free variable into a constrained one. In this case it is necessary to introduce a pair of variables. For more simplicity, we consider the example of the train timetable already seen above. Example: optimization of the train timetable The free variables πts represent the perturbations in the given times ats for each train-station pair (t,s). When the variation is a delay πts>0 and when it is an advance πts<0. If in our model we need to have only non-negative variables, then we introduce a pair of new variables π+ ts , π - ts representing the delay and the advance of train t at station s, respectively. The value of the old variable πts can be obtained from the difference π+ ts - π - ts . Another useful transformation concerns the complement of logical variables. Given a logical variable x, if we need a variable assuming complementary values, we only have to introduce a new variable x'=1-x. 5.2 Constraints So far, with the exception of the constraint relative to the definition of the discrete value variable, we considered the typical resource availability constraints (see the farmer example, the investment choice example and the burglar example). Constraints similar to these, but reversed, are those related to requirement. Example: diet Consider the problem of determining a daily diet having at our disposal different items of food, each with its own nutritional characteristics. Let us take, for instance, the following table containing the typical items of food available at the canteen of the Politecnico in Milan: Food Pasta Rice Slice of loin Carrots Potatoes Pear Calories per hg 300 250 200 70 180 100 Table 4: caloric supplies The requirement imposed by the dietician is of at least 700 calories. To express the constraint imposed by the dietician, we introduce the variables xi for the different items of food i representing the quantity of food (in hectograms) which is eaten; the constraint will be: 300 xpasta + 250 xrice + 200 xloin + 70 xcarrots + 180 xpotatoes + 100 xpear ≥ 700. Sometimes it may be helpful to transform the constraints of greater than or equal to (like the one in the diet example) or of smaller than or equal to (like those in the farmer example) into equivalent equality constraints. The transformation needs the introduction of a new variable for each constraint representing the margin with respect to requirement (in the case of ≥), or the surplus of resources

# Page 14^page=14
Federico Malucelli Introduction to Operations Research - 14 - with respect to availability (in the case of ≤). Consider the case of the manure availability constraint in the farmer problem; if we want to transform it into equality, we have: 10 xL + 20 xP + xs = 160 where the new variable xs ≥ 0 is called slack variable and gives the measure of how much resource is still available. Consider now the caloric requirement constraint in a diet; if we want to transform it into equality, we have: 300 xpasta + 250 xrice + 200 xloin + 70 xcarrots + 180 xpotatoes + 100 xpear - xs = 700 where the slack variable xs ≥ 0 gives the measure of how much we are exceeding the caloric requirement. An important class of constraints is represented by the flow constraints arising in lots of application fields, so much so that a section of this course is expressly devoted to the solution methods of this type of problems. Let us consider a simple example. Example: oil pipeline network An oilfield consisting of several wells conveys oil to refineries through a pipeline network, according to the scheme shown below: 3 1 2 4 5 Fig. 3: scheme of the oil pipeline network Nodes 1 and 2 represent wells producing 10,000 and 15,000 barrels of oil a day, respectively, while nodes 4 and 5 represent refineries demanding 13,000 and 9,000 barrels a day. Node 3 is a pumping center with no storage possibility. Arrows represent the pipes and the direction of oil pumping. The decision variables involved are the oil quantity xij to be conveyed along each pipe (i,j). If we consider well-node 1, we see that the oil quantity which is turned out cannot exceed the availability, therefore: x12 + x13 ≤ 10000. In well-node 2 the constraint is just complicated by the fact that in 2, beside the availability of its own well, we also have to consider the oil coming from node 1: x23 + x24 ≤ 15000 + x12. Similarly, refinery-nodes 5 and 4 originate the following constraints:

# Page 15^page=15
Federico Malucelli Introduction to Operations Research - 15 - x35 + x45 ≥ 9000 x24 + x34 ≥ 13000 + x45. The constraint concerning node 3 just imposes the condition that the incoming flow must be equal to the outgoing flow: x13 + x23 = x34 + x35. Exercise Transform the inequality constraints relative to wells and refineries into equalities by introducing the appropriate slack variables. Give a physical interpretation of these variables, observing that in the examined problem variables are related to oil flows. A category of constraints that often recurs in blending problems (typical of the steel industry and oil industry) is that of the so-called quality or blending constraints. Practically, it is required that a product or a by-product of the production process satisfies certain constraints about the composition quality. Example: diet In the diet case considered above, one of these constraints could be, for example, that the caloric share coming from vegetables and fruits amounts to at least 30% of the total. Since the global computation of calories depends on the solution we shall obtain, the constraint must be expressed as follows: 70 xcarrots + 180 xpotatoes + 100 xpear 300 xpasta + 250 xrice + 200 xloin + 70 xcarrots + 180 xpotatoes + 100 xpear ≥ 0.3. But unfortunately, written in this way, the constraint is not linear like those seen above, and, as we shall see later on, non-linear constraints may give rise to models which are very difficult to approach. Anyway, observing that in order to have an optimal solution the denominator must always be positive, we can transform the constraint multiplying both terms by the expression at the denominator and simplifying in the following way: -90 xpasta - 75 xrice - 60 xloin + 49 xcarrots + 126 xpotatoes + 70 xpear ≥ 0. Constraints concerning the use of logical variables are very interesting, since they can be used to translate into mathematical terms all logical relations occurring among variables. We already introduced one of these constraints when we defined discrete value variables: in that case it was an exclusion constraint, and in fact variable wl could take exactly one of the values, something that was imposed by allowing at most one logical variable yi to have value 1. A variant could enable variable wl to take value 0 as well: something that, in the context of that example, would mean not allocating any capacity to the considered link. Then, the constraint would be: ∑ i=1 r yi ≤ 1.

# Page 16^page=16
Federico Malucelli Introduction to Operations Research - 16 - Such exclusion constraints are a bit more laborious to manage if they concern variables of a non- logical kind, so they require the introduction of additional appropriate logical variables. Example: diet Consider an exclusion constraint like the following: a well-balanced diet includes either pasta or rice, but not both of them. If the variables xpasta and xrice were of a logical kind, imposing this constraint would be equivalent to what we made above, but unfortunately here we have continuous variables representing a quantity. We have to introduce two logical variables ypasta and yrice which must take the following meaning: ypasta = ⎩⎪ ⎨ ⎪⎧1if xpasta >0 0else yrice = In order to let variables ypasta and yrice take the above meaning, we have to introduce appropriate constraints actually binding them to the value of xpasta and xrice. Suppose that in any feasible solution xpasta and xrice can have at most value Mpasta and Mrice , then the constraints relating the x and the y are: xpasta ≤ Mpasta ypasta xrice ≤ Mrice yrice ypasta, yrice ∈{0,1}. In this way, if xpasta or xrice take value greater strictly than 0, the corresponding logical variables y must have value 1 and the exclusion constraint is: ypasta + yrice ≤ 1. As we can observe, ypasta and yrice are not bound to take value 0 if the corresponding variable x has value 0. Exclusion constraints represent a particular case of logical constraint (exclusive or). Let us examine other cases, for example implications: if variable x1 has value 1, then also variable x2 must have value 1; considering variables in accordance with their logical meaning, we have the implication x1⇒x2. Keeping in mind the meaning of the implication, we see that among all configurations of the values of variables the one we have to forbid is x1=1, x2=0, which is translated into mathematical terms as: x1 ≤ x2. Negation too can be easily translated into mathematical terms using the complement of 1, as we saw with variables. So, for example, the implication x1⇒¬ x2 is translated as: x1 ≤ (1-x2), hence x1 + x2 ≤ 1.

Let A be a formula in Conjunctive Normal Form (CNF): A = C1 ∧ C2 ∧ ... ∧ Cm, where C1, C2, ..., Cm are clauses of the kind Ci = ±P1∨±P2∨...∨±Pr, and ±Pj is used to indicate either Pj or its negation ¬Pj, j=1,…, n. A classical problem in logic aims at determining, if one exists, a truth value for the propositions P1 , P2 , Pn that makes true the formula A. Such problem is known as Satisfiability Problem. Note that the satisfiability problem is not really an optimization problem, since there is there is no objective function to be maximized or minimized, although its combinatorial nature is evident. An optimization variant is the one known as maximum satisfiability, in which the objective is to maximize the number of satisfied clauses (or to minimize the number of non-satisfied clauses). A formula is satisfiable if the optimal value of the maximum satisfiability problem is equal to the number of clauses. Consider the clause: P1 ∨ ¬P2 ∨ P3 ∨ ¬P4 stating that at least one of the literals P1, ¬P2, P3 or ¬P4 is true. Example: location of base radio stations When planning a mobile telecommunications network, it is necessary to install antennas of base radio stations choosing among a set of candidate sites S={1,…,m}, so as to serve a set of customers C={1,…,n}. The variables involved are those representing the choice of sites where antennas are installed: yj has value 1 if an antenna is placed in site j and 0 else. Further, we have variables xij assigning customers to antennas, (xij=1 if the customer i is served by antenna j and 0 else). Constraints concern the fact that each customer must be served: ∑ j∈S xij = 1 ∀i∈C. The second way of representing coherence constraints takes into account each customer-antenna pair: xij ≤ yj ∀i∈C, ∀j∈S. In this case too we have to do with an implication: if i is assigned to j, then j has to get an antenna installed. From the modeling point of view, these two ways of representing coherence constraints are equivalent. But if we consider the solution efficiency, the second type of formulation, in spite of the greater number of constraints, enables the solvers of Integer Linear Programming problems to be more efficient. When approaching a real problem of optimization it very frequently happens that the objective being pursued is not only one but are several and often in contrast with each other. This is a case of multi-objective programming. Let us analyze two ways of approaching such cases by using a variant of the preceding example. Example: location of base radio stations taking into account the implementation cost In the preceding example we focused on the aspects related to power; now we consider the network implementation cost and pursue the objective of minimizing it. Therefore, differently from the preceding example, we consider an installation cost cj>0 for each candidate site j. The problem constraints remain unchanged, whereas the objective function considers the costs and becomes: min ∑ j∈S cj yj. Now we consider a situation in which it is not required that the totality of all users is covered, so that the covering constraint from equality becomes inequality: ∑ j∈S xij ≤ 1 ∀i∈C. The optimization problem minimizing the installation cost, without the constraint of covering all users, has obviously as optimal solution the null solution. So, we can pursue the second objective of maximizing the number of served customers, which is in contrast with the objective of minimizing the cost. There are two ways of considering two (or more) objective functions. The first way tries to reduce the two functions to the same scale of values by putting both criteria on the same plane and by including them in only one utility function. In the example of the mobile telecommunications network we introduce a parameter α quantifying in economic terms the advantage of having a new connected user. Thus, the utility function becomes:

The differences between the various languages are very slight, therefore switching from one to the other is easy. There are different ways of using the language to write a Linear Programming model. The best is to be able to write in such a way as to make the code as legible as possible and, moreover, to ensure that it is easy to perform any change that might be necessary. Note, however, that having the model structure together with the data makes the management not much flexible. In order to make the model parametric, so as not to be forced to rewrite the whole code at the slightest data change, we separate the problem structure as such (file .mod in AMPL) from the data (file .dat in AMPL). A fundamental element playing an essential role in the model description is the structure of sets (keyword “set” in AMPL). This is because sets enable to index variables, constraints and parameters of the model. Symbolical names for all the problem parameters will be introduced as well, in a way somehow similar to what we did writing the problem in matricial form. Let us consider again the farmer problem. Example: farmer (continuation) In this case the sets to be introduced are two: a set referring to variables and performances that we may call “cultures”, and a set to be referred to constraints that we may call “resources”. The parameters are: the returns per hectare (vector c) indexed per culture; the resource absorption (matrix A) indexed per resource and per culture; the resource availability (vector b), obviously indexed per resource. We name the variables x by indexing them on the cultures. In the declaration of the variables it is possible to indicate the upper or lower bounds, for example the sign constraints. So the file farmer.mod is the following: set cultures; set resources; param return{cultures}; param availability{resources}; param absorption{resources,cultures}; var x{cultures}>=0; maximize profit: sum{j in cultures} return[j]*x[j]; subject to bound_resources{i in resources}: sum{j in cultures} absorption[i,j]*x[j] <= availability[i]; File farmer.mod Note how it has been possible to assign a name to the objective function (profit) as well as to each constraint (bound_resources indexed on resources).
